```{r setup}
#| include: false
# =====================================================================
# SETUP — reads every committed results CSV and builds `V`, a named list
# of PRE-FORMATTED, ASSERT-GUARDED strings. Every inline statistic in the
# prose below is `V$name`; NO statistic is hand-typed. Tables are rendered
# directly from the CSVs via kable (values come from the files, not typed).
# results/ is READ-ONLY input. If a guard fails, the render fails — that is
# the enforcement mechanism the dispatch asks for.
# =====================================================================
suppressWarnings(suppressMessages({ library(here); library(jsonlite) }))
res <- function(...) here::here("results", ...)
figp <- function(...) here::here("figures", ...)

fmt <- function(x, k = 2) formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = k)
ci  <- function(lo, hi, k = 2) paste0("[", fmt(lo, k), ", ", fmt(hi, k), "]")
# assert round(x,k)==target (guard the value), then return x
gd  <- function(x, target, k) { stopifnot(abs(round(as.numeric(x), k) - target) < 1e-9); as.numeric(x) }
cell <- function(df, col, ...) {
  cd <- list(...); keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(df))
  for (nm in names(cd)) keep <- keep & (df[[nm]] == cd[[nm]])
  v <- df[[col]][keep]; stopifnot(length(v) == 1L); as.numeric(v)
}

# ---- load ----
prov  <- fromJSON(res("step0a_provenance.json"))
coefs <- read.csv(res("step0b2_SIMULATION_calibration_coefs.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
evsum <- read.csv(res("step0b2_SIMULATION_eval_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
step1 <- read.csv(res("step1_REALDATA_domain_summary.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rel2  <- read.csv(res("step2_REALDATA_reliability.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tn2   <- read.csv(res("step2_REALDATA_trialsneeded.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s6    <- read.csv(res("step6_REALDATA_confirmatory.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s7    <- read.csv(res("step7_REALDATA_descriptive.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s9    <- read.csv(res("step9_REALDATA_step4_multilevel.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s9i   <- read.csv(res("step9_REALDATA_ipsative_exhibit.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s8i   <- read.csv(res("step8_SIMULATION_ipsative_exhibit.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sel   <- read.csv(res("step11_CONFDB_selection.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
inv   <- read.csv(res("step11_CONFDB_inventory.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rel11 <- read.csv(res("step11_CONFDB_reliability.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
prov11<- fromJSON(res("step11_CONFDB_provenance.json"))
man11 <- read.csv(res("step11_CONFDB_manifest.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s14   <- read.csv(res("step14_SIMULATION_confdb_nullref.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
s15   <- read.csv(res("step15_CONFDB_contrast.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
claim <- read.csv(res("step17_claim_status.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

V <- list()

# ---- provenance ----
V$lund_md5    <- prov$files$trial$md5; stopifnot(V$lund_md5 == "500b2e6e1eb0e47e717feba5b912ad9f")
V$lund_commit <- prov$pinned_commit
V$lund_n      <- prov$structure$n_subjects; stopifnot(V$lund_n == 322)
V$lund_rows   <- format(prov$structure$n_rows, big.mark = ","); stopifnot(prov$structure$n_rows == 193200)
V$lund_conf   <- paste(range(prov$structure$confidence_values), collapse = "-")

# ---- calibration (200/200) ----
ca <- gd(coefs$intercept_a[coefs$config == "200/200"], 0.040, 3)
cb <- gd(coefs$slope_b[coefs$config == "200/200"], 0.749, 3)
V$calib_a <- fmt(ca, 4); V$calib_b <- fmt(cb, 4)

# ---- power at true gap 0.4, 200/200 ----
gp <- evsum[evsum$scenario == "GAP" & evsum$config == "200/200" & evsum$suite == "eval_main", ]
V$power <- fmt(gd((gp$n_rep - gp$gap_c_ci_zero) / gp$n_rep, 0.60, 2) * 100, 0)

# ---- reliability floor (Lund) ----
sh <- rel2[rel2$kind == "splithalf_SB", ]
lv <- sh[sh$measure == "mean_conf", ]; au <- sh[sh$measure == "auroc2", ]
V$lund_level_rng <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(lv$reliability), 0.949, 3)), "-", fmt(gd(max(lv$reliability), 0.988, 3)))
V$lund_auroc_rng <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(au$reliability), 0.390, 3)), "-", fmt(gd(max(au$reliability), 0.837, 3)))
pr <- rel2[rel2$kind == "parcel_reliability" & rel2$measure == "auroc2", ]
V$parc_mem <- fmt(gd(pr$reliability[pr$domain == "memory"], 0.546, 3))
V$parc_vis <- fmt(gd(pr$reliability[pr$domain == "vision"], 0.273, 3))
V$parc_cal <- fmt(gd(pr$reliability[pr$domain == "Calories"], 0.306, 3))
V$parc_gdp <- fmt(gd(pr$reliability[pr$domain == "GDP"], 0.242, 3))

# ---- trials-needed (rel .7) ----
t7 <- function(dom, m) tn2$trials_to_.7[tn2$domain == dom & tn2$measure == m]
V$tn_level_lo <- fmt(gd(t7("vision", "mean_conf"), 7.28, 2), 0)
V$tn_level_hi <- fmt(gd(t7("memory", "mean_conf"), 14.61, 2), 0)
V$tn_auroc_mem <- fmt(gd(t7("memory", "auroc2"), 106.32, 2), 0)
V$tn_auroc_vis <- fmt(gd(t7("vision", "auroc2"), 362.14, 2), 0)

# ---- confirmatory (step6) ----
# PRECISION CONVENTION (dispatch 012): the confirmatory gap (point + its CIs)
# renders at 3 dp to match the claim-status table and Figure 1 caption; all
# other in-text correlations render at 2 dp (fmt/ci default k = 2).
c6 <- function(q, col) cell(s6, col, block = "PRIMARY_CONFIRMATORY", quantity = q)
V$gap      <- fmt(gd(c6("gap_corrected", "estimate"), 0.113, 3), 3)
V$gap_ci   <- ci(c6("gap_corrected", "ci_lo"), c6("gap_corrected", "ci_hi"), 3)
V$rl       <- fmt(gd(c6("rho_level_latent", "estimate"), 0.422, 3))
V$rl_ci    <- ci(c6("rho_level_latent", "ci_lo"), c6("rho_level_latent", "ci_hi"))
V$rs       <- fmt(gd(c6("rho_sens_latent_corrected", "estimate"), 0.308, 3))
V$rs_ci    <- ci(c6("rho_sens_latent_corrected", "ci_lo"), c6("rho_sens_latent_corrected", "ci_hi"))
V$n_conf   <- as.character(cell(s6, "n", block = "PRIMARY_CONFIRMATORY", quantity = "gap_corrected"))
# secondary c: uncorrected latent
V$rs_unc   <- fmt(gd(cell(s6, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_c_uncorrected", quantity = "rho_sens_latent_uncorrected"), 0.271, 3))
V$rs_unc_ci<- ci(cell(s6, "ci_lo", block = "SECONDARY_c_uncorrected", quantity = "rho_sens_latent_uncorrected"),
                 cell(s6, "ci_hi", block = "SECONDARY_c_uncorrected", quantity = "rho_sens_latent_uncorrected"))
V$gap_unc  <- fmt(gd(cell(s6, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_c_uncorrected", quantity = "gap_uncorrected"), 0.150, 3))
# secondary a: bootstrap gap CI (3 dp — same gap, convention above)
V$gap_boot_ci <- ci(cell(s6, "ci_lo", block = "SECONDARY_a_bootstrap", quantity = "gap_corrected_bootCI"),
                    cell(s6, "ci_hi", block = "SECONDARY_a_bootstrap", quantity = "gap_corrected_bootCI"), 3)
# exhibit d: naive raw
V$rawL <- fmt(gd(cell(s6, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_r_mean_conf"), 0.402, 3))
V$rawS <- fmt(gd(cell(s6, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_r_auroc2"), 0.202, 3))
V$rawgap <- fmt(gd(cell(s6, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_gap_naive"), 0.200, 3))
V$rawgap_ci <- ci(cell(s6, "ci_lo", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_gap_naive"),
                  cell(s6, "ci_hi", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_gap_naive"))
V$n_exhib <- as.character(cell(s6, "n", block = "SECONDARY_d_manifest_EXHIBIT", quantity = "raw_gap_naive"))

# ---- descriptive (step7) ----
V$d_rl_rng  <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(s7$rho_level), 0.323, 3)), "-", fmt(gd(max(s7$rho_level), 0.473, 3)))
V$d_visgdp_gap <- fmt(gd(s7$gap_uncorrected[s7$pair == "vision_x_GDP"], 0.296, 3))
V$d_visgdp_lo  <- fmt(gd(s7$gap_lo[s7$pair == "vision_x_GDP"], 0.055, 3))
V$d_visgdp_band <- fmt(gd(s7$bias_band[s7$pair == "vision_x_GDP"], 0.09, 2))
V$d_memgdp_gap <- fmt(gd(s7$gap_uncorrected[s7$pair == "memory_x_GDP"], -0.133, 3))

# ---- multilevel (step9) ----
V$icc_l <- fmt(gd(cell(s9, "estimate", quantity = "ICC_level"), 0.443, 3))
V$icc_s <- fmt(gd(cell(s9, "estimate", quantity = "ICC_sens"), 0.337, 3))
V$dicc  <- fmt(gd(cell(s9, "estimate", quantity = "Delta_ICC"), 0.105, 3))
V$dicc_ci <- ci(cell(s9, "ci_lo", quantity = "Delta_ICC"), cell(s9, "ci_hi", quantity = "Delta_ICC"), 3)
V$icc_l2 <- fmt(cell(s9, "ci_lo", quantity = "ICC_level"), 2)
V$ips_real_min <- fmt(gd(min(s9i$r_centered), -0.667, 3))
V$ips_real_max <- fmt(gd(max(s9i$r_centered), 0.083, 3))
V$ips_real_mean <- fmt(gd(mean(s9i$r_centered), -0.298, 3))
V$ips_sim_mean <- fmt(gd(mean(s8i$r_centered[s8i$replicate == 1]), -0.31, 2), 2)

# ---- CD selection funnel ----
V$cd_parsed <- as.character(sum(inv$parse_status == "OK")); stopifnot(V$cd_parsed == "180")
V$cd_multi  <- as.character(sum(inv$multi_task_within_subject == TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)); stopifnot(V$cd_multi == "21")
V$cd_sel    <- as.character(sum(sel$selected)); stopifnot(V$cd_sel == "4")
V$cd_bytes  <- format(prov11$total_bytes_verified, big.mark = ",")
V$cd_mismatch <- as.character(prov11$n_md5_mismatch)
V$cd_nonv1  <- as.character(sum(man11$osf_version != 1))
V$cd_seldata_v1 <- all(man11$osf_version[man11$role == "data" &
  man11$filename %in% paste0("data_", c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2","Arbuzova_unpub_3","Bang_2019_Exp2","Haddara_2022_Expt1"), ".csv")] == 1)
stopifnot(V$cd_seldata_v1)

# ---- CD reliability ranges ----
V$cd_level_rng <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(rel11$rel_sb[rel11$measure=="level"]),0.970,3)), "-",
                         fmt(gd(max(rel11$rel_sb[rel11$measure=="level"]),0.996,3)))
V$cd_auroc_rng <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(rel11$rel_sb[rel11$measure=="auroc2"]),0.615,3)), "-",
                         fmt(gd(max(rel11$rel_sb[rel11$measure=="auroc2"]),0.903,3)))

# ---- CD contrast headline (step15) ----
rl15 <- function(study) cell(s15, "estimate", study=study, quantity="r_level", subset="primary", tier="PRIMARY")
V$cd_arbU_rl <- fmt(gd(rl15("Arbuzova_unpub_3"), 0.560, 3))
V$cd_arbU_rl_ci <- ci(cell(s15,"ci_lo",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="r_level",subset="primary",tier="PRIMARY"),
                      cell(s15,"ci_hi",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="r_level",subset="primary",tier="PRIMARY"))
V$cd_arbU_rs <- fmt(gd(cell(s15,"estimate",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="r_sens",subset="primary",tier="PRIMARY"), -0.097, 3))
arbU_rawgap <- gd(cell(s15,"estimate",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="gap_raw",subset="primary",tier="SECONDARY"), 0.551, 3)
arbU_n30 <- gd(cell(s15,"nullref_rho30_hi",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="gap_raw",subset="primary",tier="SECONDARY"), 0.505, 3)
arbU_n45 <- gd(cell(s15,"nullref_rho45_hi",study="Arbuzova_unpub_3",quantity="gap_raw",subset="primary",tier="SECONDARY"), 0.531, 3)
V$cd_arbU_rawgap <- fmt(arbU_rawgap, 3)
V$cd_arbU_n30 <- fmt(arbU_n30, 3); V$cd_arbU_n45 <- fmt(arbU_n45, 3)
V$cd_margin30 <- fmt(gd(round(arbU_rawgap,3) - round(arbU_n30,3), 0.046, 3), 3)
V$cd_margin45 <- fmt(gd(round(arbU_rawgap,3) - round(arbU_n45,3), 0.020, 3), 3)
V$cd_hadd_rs <- fmt(gd(cell(s15,"estimate",study="Haddara_2022_Expt1",quantity="r_sens",subset="primary",tier="PRIMARY"), 0.561, 3))
V$cd_rl_lo <- fmt(min(sapply(c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2","Arbuzova_unpub_3","Bang_2019_Exp2","Haddara_2022_Expt1"), rl15)),2)
V$cd_rl_hi <- fmt(max(sapply(c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2","Arbuzova_unpub_3","Bang_2019_Exp2","Haddara_2022_Expt1"), rl15)),2)
V$cd_arbU_n <- as.character(unique(s15$n_subjects[s15$study == "Arbuzova_unpub_3" & s15$subset == "primary"]))
stopifnot(V$cd_arbU_n == "40")

# ---- MLE external cross-check (Methods §data): guard the >=0.998 claim ----
# provenance JSON per-subject own-vs-shipped correlations, one per domain.
mlecor <- prov$per_subject_agreement$cor_own_vs_shipped
V$mle_cor_rng <- paste0(fmt(gd(min(mlecor), 0.998, 3), 3), "-", fmt(gd(max(mlecor), 0.999, 3), 3))

# ---- Step-4 robustness quartet (R1 z-scored, R2 ordinal); guard hand-typed vals ----
s9d <- read.csv(res("step9_REALDATA_step4_diagnostics.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
r1 <- function(q) cell(s9d, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_R1_zscored", quantity = q)
r2 <- function(q) cell(s9d, "estimate", block = "SECONDARY_R2_ordinal", quantity = q)
V$r1_icc_l <- fmt(gd(r1("ICC_level"), 0.438, 3), 2)
V$r1_icc_s <- fmt(gd(r1("ICC_sens"),  0.356, 3), 2)
V$r2_icc_l <- fmt(gd(r2("ICC_level"), 0.426, 3), 2)
V$r2_icc_s <- fmt(gd(r2("ICC_sens"),  0.324, 3), 2)

# ---- frozen systematic-bias bands (for inline Figure 1 caption) ----
V$band_200100 <- fmt(gd(s7$bias_band[s7$pair == "vision_x_GDP"],   0.09, 2), 2)
V$band_calgdp <- fmt(gd(s7$bias_band[s7$pair == "Calories_x_GDP"], 0.10, 2), 2)

# ============ full figure captions inline (every numeral a guarded V$) ============
# Built here from the guarded V$ strings and referenced via `#| fig-cap: !expr`.
# Design constants (trial configs 200/100, null rho 0.30/0.45, 2.5-97.5% span,
# CI level) are method parameters, not estimated statistics, and appear as text.
V$cap_fig1 <- paste0(
  "Cross-domain correlation landscape. Top: latent correlation of confidence ",
  "level (set-point) for each of the six domain pairs, with 95% delta-method ",
  "CIs. Bottom: the gap (rho_level - rho_sens) per pair. memory x vision ",
  "(filled point) is the preregistered CONFIRMATORY pair: its rho_sens is ",
  "calibration-corrected and its gap carries no systematic band. The five open ",
  "points are NON-CONFIRMATORY / DESCRIPTIVE: their sensitivity correlations ",
  "are uncorrected (these trial-count configurations failed the blind ",
  "calibration gate), and each gap therefore carries a shaded rectangle - the ",
  "frozen systematic-bias allowance (+/-", V$band_200100, " for 200/100-trial ",
  "pairs, +/-", V$band_calgdp, " for Calories x GDP). The shaded bands are ",
  "systematic-bias allowances, NOT confidence intervals; whiskers are sampling ",
  "CIs only. Note vision x GDP: its CI excludes 0, but its lower bound (",
  V$d_visgdp_lo, ") lies inside its +/-", V$band_200100, " band, so no ",
  "nonzero-gap claim is made for any descriptive pair. The confirmatory result ",
  "(gap = ", V$gap, ", 95% CI ", V$gap_ci, ") does not exclude a null gap.")

V$cap_figS1 <- paste0(
  "EXPLORATORY: gap vs sensitivity measurement quality. Each pair's gap (as in ",
  "Figure 1) against the geometric mean of its two domains' raw, pre-partialing ",
  "AUROC2 parcel reliabilities (memory ", V$parc_mem, ", vision ", V$parc_vis,
  ", Calories ", V$parc_cal, ", GDP ", V$parc_gdp, "). No line is fitted, no ",
  "correlation computed, no test performed: with six non-independent points ",
  "this display is EXPLORATORY. The measurement-lens reading - the ",
  "level-advantage appears where sensitivity is least reliably measured and ",
  "reverses where it is best measured (memory pairs) - is offered as ",
  "interpretation of residual attenuation, not as a tested result.")

V$cap_fig2 <- paste0(
  "Confidence Database level-vs-sensitivity contrast (NON-CONFIRMATORY, ",
  "robustness tier) with the Lund confirmatory pair for comparison. Left: ",
  "cross-task correlations of confidence LEVEL (filled) and metacognitive ",
  "sensitivity (open; CD rows d'-partialed AUROC2, Lund row ",
  "calibration-corrected) with 95% CIs; gray brackets are the r_sens ",
  "disattenuation RANGES - sensitivity ranges, never corrected point values. ",
  "Right: the RAW gap (r_level - r_sens_raw) per CD study with 95% CI, against ",
  "SIMULATION null-reference intervals - the 2.5-97.5% span of the raw gap in a ",
  "true-null world (true r_level = true r_sens = 0.30 dotted / 0.45 dashed) ",
  "matched to each study's n, trials, scale, and reliabilities. Raw gaps are ",
  "inflated by differential attenuation (level split-half reliabilities ",
  V$cd_level_rng, " vs AUROC2 ", V$cd_auroc_rng, "), so a positive raw gap is ",
  "expected even under a true null; only Arbuzova_unpub_3 memory x visual ",
  "exceeds its null-reference intervals (raw gap ", V$cd_arbU_rawgap,
  " vs upper bounds ", V$cd_arbU_n30, " / ", V$cd_arbU_n45, "). This tier tests ",
  "TASK-generalization with exactly one external cross-domain pair: only ",
  "Arbuzova_unpub_3 memory x visual is cross-DOMAIN; Arbuzova_2021_expt2 is a ",
  "visuomotor condition x condition pair, and Bang_2019_Exp2 and ",
  "Haddara_2022_Expt1 are within-vision task pairs - these four studies are not ",
  "four cross-domain replications. The Lund row is the preregistered ",
  "CONFIRMATORY (corrected) result: its gap (", V$gap, ", 95% CI ", V$gap_ci,
  ") does not exclude a null. Null-reference intervals are a simulation ",
  "reference, not a correction and not a test.")

# ============ helper tables (rendered from CSV, not hand-typed) ============
# reliability floor table (Lund domains)
# NOTE: sapply() returns a NAMED vector; without unname()/row.names=NULL those
# names become data-frame row names and kable prints them as a phantom column.
rel_tbl <- data.frame(
  Domain = c("Memory","Vision","Calories","GDP"),
  `Level (mean conf.)` = unname(sapply(c("memory","vision","Calories","GDP"),
    function(d) fmt(sh$reliability[sh$measure=="mean_conf" & sh$domain==d],2))),
  `Sensitivity (AUROC2)` = unname(sapply(c("memory","vision","Calories","GDP"),
    function(d) fmt(sh$reliability[sh$measure=="auroc2" & sh$domain==d],2))),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)

# descriptive 5-pair table
prettypair <- function(p) gsub("_x_", " x ", p)
desc_tbl <- data.frame(
  Pair = prettypair(s7$pair),
  `rho_level [95% CI]` = paste0(fmt(s7$rho_level), " ", ci(s7$rho_level_lo, s7$rho_level_hi)),
  `rho_sens (uncorr.) [95% CI]` = paste0(fmt(s7$rho_sens_uncorrected), " ", ci(s7$rho_sens_lo, s7$rho_sens_hi)),
  `gap [95% CI]` = paste0(fmt(s7$gap_uncorrected), " ", ci(s7$gap_lo, s7$gap_hi)),
  `band` = paste0("+/-", fmt(s7$bias_band,2)),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# CD primary contrast table
cdp <- s15[s15$subset=="primary" & s15$tier=="PRIMARY", ]
studies <- c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2","Arbuzova_unpub_3","Bang_2019_Exp2","Haddara_2022_Expt1")
getq <- function(study,q,col="estimate") cdp[[col]][cdp$study==study & cdp$quantity==q]
# Short display labels keep Study out of the n / r_level columns (the long keys
# forced a line break that collided those columns in the Typst render). The map is
# assert-guarded so an unexpected study id fails the render rather than mislabelling.
studylab <- c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2"="Arbuzova 2021 E2", "Arbuzova_unpub_3"="Arbuzova unpub 3",
              "Bang_2019_Exp2"="Bang 2019 E2", "Haddara_2022_Expt1"="Haddara 2022 E1")
pairlab <- c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2"="task1 x task2 (visuomotor, condition x condition)",
             "Arbuzova_unpub_3"="memory x visual (CROSS-DOMAIN)",
             "Bang_2019_Exp2"="task1 x task2 (coarse x fine Gabor, within vision)",
             "Haddara_2022_Expt1"="task1 x task2 (letter x color grids, within vision)")
verdict <- c("Arbuzova_2021_expt2"="partial","Arbuzova_unpub_3"="holds (narrowly)",
             "Bang_2019_Exp2"="partial","Haddara_2022_Expt1"="partial")
nsub <- sapply(studies, function(s) unique(cdp$n_subjects[cdp$study==s]))
stopifnot(all(studies %in% names(studylab)))
cd_tbl <- data.frame(
  Study = unname(studylab[studies]), Pair = unname(pairlab[studies]), n = unname(nsub),
  `r_level [95% CI]` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) paste0(fmt(getq(s,"r_level"))," ",ci(getq(s,"r_level","ci_lo"),getq(s,"r_level","ci_hi"))))),
  `r_sens (d'-part.) [95% CI]` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) paste0(fmt(getq(s,"r_sens"))," ",ci(getq(s,"r_sens","ci_lo"),getq(s,"r_sens","ci_hi"))))),
  `verdict` = unname(verdict[studies]),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)

# CD yardstick table (raw gap vs null-reference + disatt ranges)
raw <- s15[s15$subset=="primary" & s15$tier=="SECONDARY" & s15$quantity=="gap_raw", ]
disL <- s15[s15$subset=="primary" & s15$tier=="PRIMARY" & s15$quantity=="r_level", ]
disS <- s15[s15$subset=="primary" & s15$tier=="PRIMARY" & s15$quantity=="r_sens", ]
yard_tbl <- data.frame(
  Study = unname(studylab[studies]),
  `r_level disatt. range` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) ci(disL$disatt_lo[disL$study==s],disL$disatt_hi[disL$study==s]))),
  `r_sens disatt. range`  = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) ci(disS$disatt_lo[disS$study==s],disS$disatt_hi[disS$study==s]))),
  `raw gap [95% CI]` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) paste0(fmt(raw$estimate[raw$study==s])," ",ci(raw$ci_lo[raw$study==s],raw$ci_hi[raw$study==s])))),
  `null-ref (rho=.30)` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) ci(raw$nullref_rho30_lo[raw$study==s],raw$nullref_rho30_hi[raw$study==s]))),
  `null-ref (rho=.45)` = unname(sapply(studies,function(s) ci(raw$nullref_rho45_lo[raw$study==s],raw$nullref_rho45_hi[raw$study==s]))),
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)

# claim-status summary table for Results (subset of columns)
# The full tier strings are 30-40 characters and wrapped into a column so narrow
# that rows collided across the page break. Short codes carry the same information;
# the dagger and the key are spelled out in the caption. Guarded: an unmapped tier
# fails the render. VALUES are untouched -- only the tier LABEL is abbreviated, and
# estimates/CIs are formatted (not retyped) from the committed CSV.
tiermap <- c("CONFIRMATORY" = "Confirmatory",
             "METHODS EXHIBIT" = "Methods exhibit",
             "DESCRIPTIVE (NON-CONFIRMATORY)" = "Descriptive*",
             "STEP4 MULTILEVEL (NON-CONFIRMATORY)" = "Multilevel*",
             "CONFDB ROBUSTNESS (NON-CONFIRMATORY)" = "ConfDB*",
             "FLOOR / METHODS" = "Floor / methods")
stopifnot(all(claim$tier %in% names(tiermap)))
num3 <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))), NA_character_,
                           formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = 3))
est3 <- num3(claim$estimate); lo3 <- num3(claim$ci_lo); hi3 <- num3(claim$ci_hi)
claim_tbl <- data.frame(
  `#` = seq_len(nrow(claim)),
  `Claim` = gsub("_", " ", claim$claim_id),
  `Tier` = unname(tiermap[claim$tier]),
  `Estimate [95% CI]` = ifelse(is.na(est3), "-",
                ifelse(is.na(lo3), est3, paste0(est3, " [", lo3, ", ", hi3, "]"))),
  `Verdict (frozen)` = claim$verdict_wording,
  check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL)

kb <- function(df, cap) knitr::kable(df, caption = cap, align = "l")
```

# Abstract {#sec-abstract}

Confidence in one's own judgements correlates across cognitive domains, a
pattern usually read as evidence for domain-general metacognitive ability. But
"confidence" conflates two separable quantities: its LEVEL — a person's average
confidence, or set-point — and its INFORMATIVENESS, the metacognitive
sensitivity with which confidence discriminates correct from incorrect
responses. Because level is measured far more reliably than sensitivity, a naive
comparison of their cross-domain correlations manufactures an apparent
level-over-sensitivity advantage even when none exists. Using a preregistered,
reliability-corrected estimator validated by simulation before it touched the
data, we ask which component is domain-general in a four-domain confidence study
[@Lund_2025]. Confidence level generalizes strongly across domains
(ρ_level = `r V$rl`). Corrected metacognitive sensitivity also correlates across
domains (ρ_sens = `r V$rs`, 95% CI excluding zero) — it is not domain-specific.
The level-minus-sensitivity gap that a strong dissociation account predicts is
`r V$gap`, with a 95% CI that does not exclude zero; the same analysis without
correction would have "confirmed" a dissociation (raw gap `r V$rawgap`,
excluding zero). A non-ipsative multilevel decomposition and an external
robustness tier across four Confidence Database studies reproduce the pattern:
level travels, while the dissociation does not survive attenuation-aware
analysis. Apparent dissociations between confidence components in metacognition
are, in substantial part, a measurement-reliability artifact.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

People are, to a degree, aware of when they are right and when they are wrong,
and they express that awareness as confidence in their own judgements
[@Fleming_2014]. A striking regularity in the metacognition literature is that
confidence appears to travel across otherwise unrelated tasks: someone who
reports high or well-calibrated confidence about a perceptual judgement tends to
do so about a memory judgement as well. This cross-domain coherence is widely
taken as evidence for a domain-general metacognitive faculty — a single
self-monitoring capacity that operates over the outputs of many different
cognitive systems. Whether such a general capacity exists, and what exactly it
would consist of, matters both for theories of metacognition and for the
practical hope that a person's self-assessment in one setting tells us something
about their self-assessment in another.

The difficulty is that "confidence" is not one thing. A confidence report
carries at least two separable quantities. The first is its LEVEL, or set-point:
how high a person runs the dial on average — a response-style or scale-use
tendency that is largely independent of whether the confidence is deserved. The
second is its INFORMATIVENESS, or metacognitive sensitivity: how well a person's
confidence discriminates their own correct from incorrect responses. These can
dissociate in principle, and they support very different claims. A shared
set-point across domains is a domain-general *bias* — a person who simply tends
to feel sure of themselves everywhere. A shared sensitivity across domains is a
domain-general *skill* — a genuine self-monitoring ability that generalizes.
Much prior work reports cross-domain confidence correlations without cleanly
separating these two, so it is often unclear which of the two — bias or skill —
the reported generality actually reflects.

This ambiguity would be a minor definitional matter were it not compounded by a
measurement hazard that runs in a specific direction. Confidence level is
measured almost perfectly from a modest number of trials, because it is just an
average. Metacognitive sensitivity, by contrast, is estimated from the
covariation between confidence and accuracy within a person, is bounded by the
number of trials available, and is measured poorly at realistic trial counts. A
difference between two correlations is biased upward when one of the two
variables is measured much more reliably than the other. It follows that a raw,
uncorrected comparison of level-generalization against sensitivity-generalization
will tend to *manufacture* an apparent advantage of level over sensitivity even
when the two are equally domain-general in truth. Any honest test of whether the
domain-general part of confidence is its level rather than its informativeness
must therefore confront differential reliability head-on, rather than reading a
raw gap between two correlations at face value. This measurement hazard is the
pivot around which the present paper is built.

We take a deliberately conservative, from-scratch approach. Before computing any
cross-domain quantity, we build and validate a two-component measurement layer in
simulation, requiring that each component's estimator recovers its known planted
value and that the two components are separable — that estimating one does not
leak into the other. That gate forces two design choices that are not cosmetic:
metacognitive sensitivity must be partialed for first-order performance, and one
domain pair alone meets the trial-count requirement for a calibrated,
reliability-corrected confirmatory test. Around that single preregistered test
we place explicitly weaker tiers — a descriptive survey of the remaining domain
pairs with frozen bias allowances, a non-ipsative multilevel decomposition that
avoids the mean-subtraction artifact known to plague this literature, and an
external robustness tier drawn from an independent multi-study database — each
carried with attenuation-aware yardsticks rather than raw comparisons. We keep a
firewall between building the measurement layer and testing the thesis, and we
fix the reporting wording in advance. We state plainly at the outset that a null
or partial dissociation is an acceptable, reportable outcome: the design is
powered to detect a substantial level-over-sensitivity gap, not a small one, and
we report what the data show either way.

This paper makes four contributions. First, a validated two-component
measurement framework for confidence with an explicit recovery-and-separability
gate, so that the estimators are known to work before they are trusted. Second, a
preregistered, reliability-corrected confirmatory test of which component is
domain-general in the four-domain study of @Lund_2025. Third, a non-ipsative
multilevel decomposition that asks which component carries the cross-domain
covariance without inducing the ipsative artifact of naive mean subtraction.
Fourth, an external robustness tier across four multi-task studies from the
Confidence Database [@Rahnev_2020], each read against a simulated null reference
rather than pooled. The thesis these tiers converge on is a measurement-lens one:
what looks, in prior-style analyses, like a dissociation in which confidence
level generalizes and metacognitive sensitivity does not is, once measurement
reliability is handled honestly, largely absent as a *distinguishable* effect —
while confidence level itself clearly does generalize across domains.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Primary dataset and provenance {#sec-methods-data}

The primary data are the trial-level records of @Lund_2025, a confirmatory
multi-domain metacognition study spanning four domains — episodic memory,
visual perception, and two semantic-knowledge judgements (Calories and GDP).
We re-fetched the trial file directly from the authors' public repository at
a pinned commit (`r substr(V$lund_commit,1,10)`…) and verified it before
any use: the MD5 checksum matched the value recorded by the authors
(`r V$lund_md5`), and the structure matched expectation —
`r V$lund_rows` trials from `r V$lund_n` subjects across the four
domains, with confidence reported on a `r V$lund_conf` scale. As an
external cross-check (never as a primary number) we reproduced per-subject
mean confidence against the authors' shipped MLE fits; agreement was high
(within-domain correlations `r V$mle_cor_rng` across the four domains), the
small residual reflecting their undocumented preprocessing. Median trials per subject are 200 for memory and
vision and roughly 100 for the two knowledge domains. Following the
from-scratch mandate of this project, all analysis code is original to this
repository and no computational result from any prior effort was reused or
consulted; every reported number is computed in code from the verified raw
data.

## The two components and their measures {#sec-methods-measures}

We operationalize confidence LEVEL (set-point) as the subject's
scale-normalized mean confidence within a domain, and metacognitive
SENSITIVITY (informativeness) as AUROC2 — the area under the type-2 ROC
[@Galvin_2003; @Fleming_2014], a model-light index of how well confidence
discriminates a person's own correct from incorrect responses. We treat the
signal-detection meta-d′/M-ratio family [@Maniscalco_2012] as secondary
rather than the spine of the paper, consistent with the model-light posture
of this project. Because
AUROC2 is confounded by first-order performance (d′), **every sensitivity
claim in this paper is d′-partialed**: sensitivity is the residual of AUROC2
after regressing out same-domain d′. This choice is not cosmetic — it was
forced by the Step 0 gate (below), where the raw (un-partialed) latent
estimator converted a pure d′ correlation into a spurious sensitivity
correlation. We do not use gamma as a sensitivity measure: in recovery
simulation it leaked the set-point (a level-to-sensitivity contamination),
so it was dropped despite its long use as a metacognitive index
[@Nelson_1984]. The latent cross-domain correlations are estimated with an
exchangeable-parcel confirmatory factor model [@Rosseel_2012] that splits each
subject-domain's trials into parcels, giving a measurement model with a
built-in reliability correction rather than a single noisy point measure.

## Simulation-gate program (Step 0) {#sec-methods-gate}

Before testing the thesis we required a foundation gate: prove the
estimators recover known planted values, and prove the two components are
separable (estimating one does not leak into the other). The gate was run in
rounds and we report its failures honestly. The first round established that
level is recovered near-perfectly (recovery r ≈ 0.99, no leakage) but that
AUROC2 recovery is reliability-capped at realistic trial counts and that the
**raw** level-vs-sensitivity contrast manufactures a gap even under a true
null — so the naive contrast is invalid as designed. The second round showed
that a d′-partialed exchangeable-parcel latent estimator passes all criteria
at the 200/200-trial configuration but that raw-latent variants convert the
d′ confound into spurious sensitivity correlation — establishing d′-partialing
as mandatory. The final round calibrated the corrected estimator on training
seeds and evaluated it blind on fresh seeds: at 200 trials per task in both
domains the estimator passed every criterion, so the memory × vision pair
(the only pair with 200/200 trials) is the sole **confirmatory** pair; other
pairs are descriptive with explicit bias bands. The calibration coefficients
were then **frozen** (intercept a = `r V$calib_a`, slope
b = `r V$calib_b`) and never refit. A power note carried forward from
the gate: at a true gap of 0.4 and the 200/200 configuration, the corrected
test excludes zero in about `r V$power`% of simulated replicates — the
confirmatory test is powered to detect a substantial gap but not a small one.

## Confirmatory design {#sec-methods-confirmatory}

The single preregistered confirmatory test is the memory × vision pair,
chosen mechanically as the only pair meeting the gate's 200/200-trial
requirement, and fixed by git timestamp before the cross-domain quantities
were computed. We estimate the latent cross-domain correlation of level
(ρ_level) and of d′-partialed sensitivity (ρ_sens) in the parcel-CFA
framework, apply the frozen calibration correction to ρ_sens, and form the
primary outcome — the gap ρ_level − ρ_sens — with a delta-method confidence
interval; a subject bootstrap (B = 2000, calibration held fixed) is the
secondary interval. A firewall held until this step: no cross-domain
quantity of any kind was computed while the measurement layer and
reliabilities were being built. Wording is fixed in advance: a gap whose
interval includes zero is reported as **not excluded**, never as absent.

## Descriptive tier {#sec-methods-descriptive}

The other five domain pairs did not meet the 200/200 gate and are therefore
**descriptive, non-confirmatory**. For each we report ρ_level and the
**uncorrected** ρ_sens (no valid calibration exists at their trial
configurations), and we attach a frozen systematic-bias band to every gap —
±0.09 for pairs at 200/100 trials and ±0.10 for the Calories × GDP
(100/100) pair — carried directly from the gate's measured bias at those
configurations. These bands are systematic-bias allowances, not confidence
intervals; a descriptive gap is treated as consistent with zero unless it
clears both its sampling CI and its band.

## Non-ipsative multilevel decomposition (Step 4) {#sec-methods-multilevel}

The classic trap in this literature is the ipsative artifact: subtracting
each person's mean confidence mechanically induces negative between-domain
correlations, which can masquerade as a domain-specific bias. We therefore do
**not** test the thesis by mean subtraction. Instead we fit a trial-level
multilevel model [@Bates_2015] that simultaneously estimates a person-general
set-point, a person×domain set-point residual, a person-general
confidence-resolution slope (Δ confidence for correct vs. incorrect
responses, domain-accuracy centered), and a person×domain resolution
residual. From the variance components we form two generalizability indices —
ICC_level and ICC_sens, the person-general share of set-point and of
resolution variance — with cluster-bootstrap intervals (B = 500). This is a
variance-share estimand, distinct from the Step 3 latent correlation gap and
not a re-test of it. Robustness rungs re-fit with within-domain z-scored
confidence (R1) and an ordinal cumulative-link mixed model (R2). As a methods
warning we also compute what the discouraged naive mean-subtraction analysis
would have produced, on the same trials and in matched simulation, to exhibit
the artifact the model is built to avoid. The resolution slope is not
d′-partialed; the residual d′ confound is quantified in diagnostics rather
than removed, and is flagged wherever the slope is discussed.

## Confidence Database: study selection {#sec-methods-cdb-selection}

For an external robustness tier we used the Confidence Database
[@Rahnev_2020], fetched from OSF and verified file-by-file
(`r V$cd_bytes` bytes across all files; `r V$cd_mismatch` MD5
mismatches). Provenance is drawn from the committed manifest and provenance
JSON, not from any prior narrative: the live OSF node has no registered
snapshot, so it is pinned by access date and per-file version, and
`r V$cd_nonv1` files carry OSF versions above 1 (all four selected
studies' data CSVs are version 1). Study selection was mechanical and
pre-specified: of `r V$cd_parsed` parsed study files,
`r V$cd_multi` have a within-subject multi-task structure, and a
four-criterion funnel (a task pair with enough qualifying subjects and
trials; a usable confidence scale; both accuracy classes present in every
task; no structural disqualifier) selects `r V$cd_sel` studies:
Arbuzova_2021_expt2 [@Arbuzova_2021], Arbuzova_unpub_3, Bang_2019_Exp2
[@Bang_2019], and Haddara_2022_Expt1 [@Haddara_2022]. A firewall again held:
no cross-task quantity was computed during selection or measurement.

## Confidence Database: contrast and yardsticks {#sec-methods-cdb-contrast}

**Taxonomy (binding).** This tier tests TASK-generalization and contains
exactly one external cross-**domain** pair. Only Arbuzova_unpub_3
memory × visual is cross-domain. Arbuzova_2021_expt2 is a visuomotor
condition × condition pair; Bang_2019_Exp2 (coarse vs. fine Gabor) and
Haddara_2022_Expt1 (letter vs. color grids) are cross-**task** pairs within
vision. These four studies are never presented as four cross-domain
replications.

For each study we correlate confidence level across the task pair and
d′-partialed AUROC2 across the same pair (subjects with ≥ 60 clean trials in
both tasks, listwise complete; subject bootstrap B = 2000; residualization
recomputed inside every resample). Because no calibration correction exists
for these configurations, nothing in this tier is confirmatory. Two
attenuation-aware yardsticks replace the missing correction: (i) a
disattenuation **range** for each correlation (r divided by the geometric
mean of the two reliabilities, evaluated at the reliability point estimate
and both CI bounds — a sensitivity range, never a corrected point value); and
(ii) a per-study **null-reference interval** — the 2.5–97.5% span of the raw
gap in a simulated true-null world (true ρ_level = true ρ_sens) matched to
each study's n, trials, confidence scale, and reliabilities, quantifying how
much raw-gap inflation differential attenuation alone produces. The
preregistered reading rule: the Lund pattern **holds** in a study only if
r_level exceeds the top of r_sens's disattenuation range **and** the raw gap
exceeds the null-reference interval under both null scenarios; one condition
met is **partial**; neither is **fails**. No meta-analytic pooling is
performed across the four heterogeneous studies. Bang's measures were
recomputed from raw with catch trials dropped; Haddara's between-subject
feedback groups were derived from raw for a heterogeneity check only.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The measurement floor {#sec-results-floor}

Across all four Lund domains, confidence level is measured far more reliably
than metacognitive sensitivity (@tbl-reliability). Split-half
Spearman–Brown reliability [@Spearman_1910; @Brown_1910] of level ranges
`r V$lund_level_rng`, while
AUROC2 reliability ranges only `r V$lund_auroc_rng`. The gap is even
starker in trials-needed terms: reaching a reliability of 0.7 takes on the
order of `r V$tn_level_lo`–`r V$tn_level_hi` trials for level but
roughly `r V$tn_auroc_mem` (memory) to `r V$tn_auroc_vis` (vision)
trials for AUROC2. At the parcel level used by the latent model, AUROC2
reliabilities are lower still (memory `r V$parc_mem`, vision
`r V$parc_vis`, Calories `r V$parc_cal`, GDP `r V$parc_gdp`).
This asymmetry is the engine of every inflated raw gap that follows: a
difference between two correlations is biased upward when one variable is
measured much more reliably than the other.

```{r tbl-reliability}
#| label: tbl-reliability
#| tbl-cap: "Split-half (Spearman–Brown) reliability of confidence level vs. metacognitive sensitivity (AUROC2), per Lund domain. Sensitivity is measured much less reliably than level in every domain."
kb(rel_tbl, NULL)
```

## Confirmatory test: memory × vision {#sec-results-confirmatory}

**CONFIRMATORY.** In the single preregistered pair, confidence level
generalizes strongly across domains (ρ_level = `r V$rl`, 95% CI
`r V$rl_ci`). Corrected metacognitive sensitivity also correlates
across domains and its interval excludes zero (ρ_sens = `r V$rs`, 95%
CI `r V$rs_ci`) — sensitivity is not domain-specific either. The
primary outcome, the level-minus-sensitivity gap, is `r V$gap` with 95%
CI `r V$gap_ci` (n = `r V$n_conf`): **the null gap is not
excluded**. Given roughly `r V$power`% power at a true gap of 0.4, this
is a "not excluded," not an "absent." The subject bootstrap agrees
(gap CI `r V$gap_boot_ci`).

The corrected result is what keeps this honest. The uncorrected latent
sensitivity correlation is `r V$rs_unc` (95% CI `r V$rs_unc_ci`),
giving an uncorrected gap of `r V$gap_unc`; and the fully naive
subject-level analysis — raw mean-confidence correlation `r V$rawL`
minus raw AUROC2 correlation `r V$rawS` — yields a raw gap of
`r V$rawgap` with 95% CI `r V$rawgap_ci`
(n = `r V$n_exhib`) that **excludes zero**. That naive analysis would
have affirmed the thesis; the correction machinery, validated in simulation
before it touched these data, is exactly what prevented the claim
(@tbl-claims, row `naive_gap_exhibit`).

## Descriptive landscape {#sec-results-descriptive}

**DESCRIPTIVE (NON-CONFIRMATORY).** Across the five non-confirmatory pairs
(@tbl-descriptive, @fig-landscape), level generalization is uniform
(ρ_level range `r V$d_rl_rng`) while the gap is heterogeneous and
vision-anchored: positive where vision is involved, near zero or negative for
the memory × knowledge pairs. No descriptive gap clears both its sampling CI
and its systematic-bias band jointly. The most positive gap, vision × GDP
(`r V$d_visgdp_gap`), has a CI that excludes zero, but its lower bound
(`r V$d_visgdp_lo`) lies inside its ±`r V$d_visgdp_band` band, so
no nonzero-gap claim is made for it or any descriptive pair. Read through the
measurement lens (@fig-gapreliability, exploratory), the level-advantage
appears where sensitivity is least reliably measured and reverses where it is
best measured (the memory pairs) — one measurement fact, not six psychological
ones.

```{r tbl-descriptive}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive tier (NON-CONFIRMATORY): five domain pairs. rho_sens is uncorrected; each gap carries a frozen systematic-bias band. No gap clears its CI and band jointly."
kb(desc_tbl, NULL)
```

```{r fig-landscape}
#| label: fig-landscape
#| fig-cap: !expr V$cap_fig1
knitr::include_graphics(figp("fig_landscape.png"))
```

```{r fig-gapreliability}
#| label: fig-gapreliability
#| fig-cap: !expr V$cap_figS1
knitr::include_graphics(figp("figS_gap_vs_reliability.png"))
```

## Multilevel decomposition {#sec-results-multilevel}

**STEP 4 MULTILEVEL (NON-CONFIRMATORY).** The non-ipsative model apportions
confidence variance into person-general and person×domain shares. The
person-general share is `r V$icc_l` for the set-point (ICC_level) and
`r V$icc_s` for resolution (ICC_sens); their difference is
Δ_ICC = `r V$dicc` with 95% cluster-bootstrap CI `r V$dicc_ci`.
A Δ_ICC of zero sits at the very edge of this interval — we present this as a
boundary result and never claim the zero-exclusion; it is directionally
consistent with the confirmatory corrected gap (two different estimands, the
same "cannot quite exclude zero" verdict). Robustness rungs agree (R1
z-scored: ICC_level `r V$r1_icc_l`, ICC_sens `r V$r1_icc_s`; R2 ordinal:
`r V$r2_icc_l`, `r V$r2_icc_s`). The
methods exhibit confirms why mean subtraction was avoided: the naive
grand-mean-centered correlations run from `r V$ips_real_min` to
`r V$ips_real_max` (mean `r V$ips_real_mean`) in these data, and
in matched simulation the same computation manufactures a mean of about
`r V$ips_sim_mean` under a planted null (mechanical expectation ≈ −1/3),
while the multilevel model recovers the planted shares.

## External robustness: the Confidence Database {#sec-results-cdb}

**CONFDB ROBUSTNESS (NON-CONFIRMATORY).** This tier tests
task-generalization with exactly one external cross-domain pair; the
within-vision task pairs and the condition × condition pair are not
cross-domain replications. Confidence level travels well: r_level is
uniformly positive and precisely estimated across the four studies
(`r V$cd_rl_lo`–`r V$cd_rl_hi`; @tbl-cdb, @fig-cdb).
d′-partialed sensitivity is heterogeneous. Because level is measured
near-perfectly (split-half `r V$cd_level_rng`) and AUROC2 is not
(`r V$cd_auroc_rng`), a positive raw gap is expected even under a true
null, so each raw gap must be read against its simulated null-reference
interval (@tbl-cdb-yard): at these configurations, differential attenuation
plus sampling noise alone can produce raw gaps up to ~0.5 in the small-n
studies.

By the preregistered rule, the Lund pattern **holds in 1 of 4** studies,
is **partial in 3**, and **fails in 0**. In every study r_level exceeds the
top of r_sens's disattenuation range; what separates "holds" from "partial"
is whether the raw gap also clears its null reference. Only the single
external cross-domain pair does: Arbuzova_unpub_3 memory × visual
(r_level = `r V$cd_arbU_rl`, 95% CI `r V$cd_arbU_rl_ci`;
r_sens = `r V$cd_arbU_rs`) has a raw gap of `r V$cd_arbU_rawgap`
that exceeds its null-reference upper bounds (`r V$cd_arbU_n30` and
`r V$cd_arbU_n45`) — but only narrowly, by margins of
`r V$cd_margin30` and `r V$cd_margin45` against the ρ = 0.30 and
ρ = 0.45 references. This single cross-domain pair is therefore consistent
with the Lund direction and exceeds its simulated true-null reference,
narrowly; a null is not excluded in the three partial studies. Notably,
Haddara's within-vision sensitivity correlation is itself high
(r_sens = `r V$cd_hadd_rs`): metacognitive sensitivity can generalize
strongly across near-identical tasks within a domain, which is task
generalization, not cross-domain generality.

```{r tbl-cdb}
#| label: tbl-cdb
#| tbl-cap: "Confidence Database contrast (NON-CONFIRMATORY, robustness). Subject bootstrap B = 2000. Only Arbuzova_unpub_3 memory x visual is cross-domain."
#| tbl-colwidths: [13, 31, 6, 18, 20, 12]
kb(cd_tbl, NULL)
```

```{r tbl-cdb-yard}
#| label: tbl-cdb-yard
#| tbl-cap: "Attenuation-aware yardsticks: disattenuation ranges (sensitivity ranges, not corrected point values) and SIMULATION null-reference intervals for the raw gap. Only Arbuzova_unpub_3 exceeds its null-reference interval."
kb(yard_tbl, NULL)
```


## Claim-status summary {#sec-results-claims}

@tbl-claims collects every quantitative claim with its tier, estimate, and
frozen verdict wording (full machine-generated table with sources and CIs:
`results/step17_claim_status.md`).

```{r tbl-claims}
#| label: tbl-claims
```

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Read through the measurement lens, these results tell a two-sided story that
resists both of the overclaims available here. On one side, confidence level
generalizes strongly and reliably across domains: in the preregistered
confirmatory pair its cross-domain correlation is `r V$rl`, and it is uniformly
positive everywhere else we look. On the other side, once metacognitive
sensitivity is corrected for its poor reliability, it too correlates across
domains, with an interval that excludes zero (`r V$rs`) — so sensitivity is not
domain-specific either. The quantity a strong dissociation account cares about,
the level-minus-sensitivity gap, is `r V$gap` with a 95% CI of `r V$gap_ci` that
does not exclude zero. The contrast that makes the point sharpest is internal to
the same data: the naive subject-level analysis yields a gap of `r V$rawgap`
whose interval *excludes* zero and would have affirmed a dissociation, whereas
the reliability-corrected analysis of the identical subjects and domains does
not. The apparent dissociation that prior-style analyses would report is, in
substantial part, a differential-reliability artifact. This cuts in both
directions at once: against overclaiming a level-over-sensitivity dissociation,
and against the opposite conclusion that metacognitive sensitivity fails to
generalize.

The descriptive landscape across the remaining domain pairs is best read the
same way — as one measurement fact wearing several costumes rather than several
psychological facts. The level-minus-sensitivity gap is heterogeneous across
pairs: it is most positive where vision is involved and reverses to near zero or
negative for the pairs that involve memory. That pattern tracks measurement
quality rather than psychology. Metacognitive sensitivity is estimated most
reliably in memory (parcel reliability `r V$parc_mem`) and least reliably in the
other domains (vision `r V$parc_vis`, Calories `r V$parc_cal`, GDP
`r V$parc_gdp`); the apparent level advantage is largest exactly where
sensitivity is measured worst, and it shrinks or reverses where memory's
better-measured sensitivity enters the pair. We present this as an attenuation
*interpretation*, not a tested result: the gap-versus-reliability display
(@fig-gapreliability) fits no line and performs no test, and with a handful of
non-independent pairs it could not. It is worth being explicit about the one
descriptive pair whose sampling interval excludes zero, vision × GDP: its lower
bound still lies inside its frozen systematic-bias band, so even there we make no
nonzero-gap claim. The heterogeneity that a psychological account would have to
explain domain by domain is, on this reading, the shadow of a single asymmetry in
how well the two components can be measured.

The external tier from the Confidence Database adds a genuine but bounded piece
of evidence, and its structure must be stated carefully. Confidence level again
travels well: its cross-task correlation is positive and precisely estimated in
every one of the four studies (`r V$cd_rl_lo`–`r V$cd_rl_hi`). Metacognitive
sensitivity is where the taxonomy matters. Only one of the four pairs is
genuinely cross-**domain** (Arbuzova_unpub_3, memory × visual); the others are a
condition × condition pair and two within-vision task pairs, which test
task-generalization, not cross-domain generality, and are never presented as
cross-domain replications. By the preregistered rule the Lund pattern holds in
that single cross-domain pair only narrowly: its raw gap clears its simulated
null reference by margins of just `r V$cd_margin30` and `r V$cd_margin45`, so the
replication is directional rather than decisive, and a null is not excluded in
the three task-generalization pairs. Tellingly, one of those within-vision pairs
shows a strong sensitivity correlation (`r V$cd_hadd_rs`): metacognitive
sensitivity clearly *can* generalize across near-identical tasks within a domain.
That is a demonstration of task generalization, and it should not be mistaken for
evidence of cross-domain metacognitive skill — the two are different claims, and
only the former is on display here.

These results also let us reconcile the paper with the older claim that
metacognition harbours a domain-general trait. The signal that most robustly
survives across domains, in every tier, is the confidence set-point — the level
component. The multilevel decomposition tells the same story from the
variance-share side: the person-general share of the set-point (`r V$icc_l`) sits
above that of confidence resolution (`r V$icc_s`), with their difference a
boundary result that never claims to exclude zero. What this suggests is that a
good deal of what has been described as "domain-general metacognition" may be
domain-general confidence *bias* — shared scale-use, a stable set-point — rather
than a shared metacognitive *ability*. That is a more modest object than a
general self-monitoring faculty, and it is the one the present data most clearly
support; it does not deny that sensitivity generalizes, only that the evidence
here cannot cleanly separate a generalizing sensitivity from a generalizing
set-point once reliability is handled honestly.

What would settle the question the confirmatory test leaves open is more
measurement, not more theory. The corrected test is powered to detect a
substantial gap and not a small one, and metacognitive sensitivity sits on a
reliability floor throughout these data. Lifting sensitivity off that floor —
more trials per task, so that its reliability approaches the near-ceiling of
level — would let a reliability-corrected gap be estimated with far less
uncertainty. So would more genuinely cross-domain pairs, rather than the largely
within-domain task pairs that the available databases mostly offer, and
higher-powered confirmatory designs built for a small effect. The reusable
contribution of this paper is not the particular verdict in this dataset but the
machinery that produced it: a recovery-and-separability gate, an explicit
reliability correction validated before use, and simulated null references in
place of raw comparisons.

The moral generalizes beyond these four domains. Wherever two metacognitive
quantities are measured with very different reliability — and confidence level
and metacognitive sensitivity almost always are — comparing their cross-domain
correlations without correction will invite a manufactured dissociation. The
honest version of the question is not "does level generalize more than
sensitivity?" but "does it generalize more than differential attenuation alone
would predict?" In these data, once that question is asked properly, confidence
level clearly generalizes, and the apparent gap between the two components does
not survive.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Several limitations bound these conclusions. First, the confirmatory test is
powered to detect only a substantial dissociation: at a true gap of 0.4 the
corrected test excludes zero roughly `r V$power`% of the time, so the null gap we
report is "not excluded" rather than evidence of no dissociation — the design
cannot distinguish a true null from a small gap it is underpowered to find.
Second, metacognitive sensitivity is weakly measured everywhere in these data
(split-half AUROC2 reliability far below that of confidence level); we therefore
present disattenuation only as a range, never as a corrected point estimate, and
treat the reliability asymmetry as a systematic feature rather than a nuisance to
be fully removed. Third, the multilevel Δ_ICC is a boundary result: a Δ_ICC of
zero sits at the very edge of its interval, within Monte-Carlo error of the
bound, so we do not claim a zero-exclusion. Fourth, the confirmatory test rests
on a single dataset and a single 200/200-trial domain pair (memory × vision); the
other pairs are explicitly descriptive. Fifth, the external cross-domain evidence
rests on a single small study (Arbuzova_unpub_3, n = `r V$cd_arbU_n`) that clears
its simulated null reference only narrowly (margins `r V$cd_margin30` and
`r V$cd_margin45`), and the smaller margin shrinks further under an independently
constructed null simulator — so this replication is directional, not decisive;
the remaining external pairs are within-vision task pairs or a condition pair and
test task-generalization, not cross-domain generality. Sixth, the null-reference
simulator matches each study's reliabilities and means but not higher moments,
and uses fixed per-task accuracy with equally spaced latent thresholds. Seventh,
the Confidence-Database disattenuation applies AUROC2 reliabilities to the
d′-partialed residual, whose reliability is not identical to that of raw AUROC2.
Eighth, first-order sensitivity (d′) is itself poorly measured outside the memory
domain, and the multilevel resolution slope is not d′-partialed (the residual
confound is quantified, not removed). Finally, gamma was excluded as a
sensitivity measure because it leaked the set-point in recovery simulation, and
we treat the meta-d′/M-ratio family as secondary; no meta-analytic pooling is
performed across the heterogeneous Confidence-Database studies.

# Data and code availability {#sec-availability}

All analysis code is original to this project and public at
`https://github.com/dondon20201/paper2`; the analysis runs end-to-end under a
renv lockfile (R 4.6.1) [@R_base]. Every reported number is written to a file under
`results/` with a name traceable from the text, and each figure's underlying
data is saved alongside it (`results/fig_landscape_data.csv`,
`results/figS_gap_vs_reliability_data.csv`,
`results/fig_confdb_contrast_data.csv`).

**Primary data.** @Lund_2025, file
`data_summary/metacognition_trialData_master.csv` from the repository
`embodied-computation-group/dg-metacognition`, pinned at commit
`r substr(V$lund_commit,1,10)`… and verified by MD5
(`r V$lund_md5`). The raw file is not redistributed here (provenance in
`data/raw/lund2025/README.md`).

**Secondary data.** The Confidence Database [@Rahnev_2020] from OSF node
`s46pr`, verified file-by-file against OSF MD5s (`r V$cd_bytes` bytes,
`r V$cd_mismatch` mismatches); the live node has no registered
snapshot, so it is pinned by access date and per-file OSF version in
`results/step11_CONFDB_manifest.csv`. Raw Confidence Database files
(~255 MB) are not redistributed here.
